fixes.explanation: Right on the money, baker. Azariah son of Hoshaiah and Johanan son of Kareah, a commander, join the arrogant men and tell Jeremiah, “You are lying!” Jeremiah is the prophet who just handed them the very answer they asked for (Jeremiah 42:2–3). They say the LORD never sent him to tell them not to go to Egypt (Jeremiah 43:2). Friend, I've heard some excuses, but telling the messenger he made it up is a bold one.

Not quite, friend. The men don't mention work at all. They say the Chaldeans would put them to death or exile them to Babylon. That is their accusation against Baruch, Jeremiah's scribe, and the text gives us no sign he planned anything like that.

The commanders are named, but that's a long way from the whole list. The text says Johanan and the commanders took the whole remnant of Judah (Jeremiah 43:5). That includes the men, women and children, plus the king's daughters, Jeremiah and Baruch (Jeremiah 43:6). Quite the crowd for a trip nobody was told to take.

Only their own families is much too small, though. The text says the whole remnant of Judah went, including men, women, children and the king's daughters (Jeremiah 43:5-6). Jeremiah the prophet and Baruch went too. This was one very full road, baker.
Memphis is a fair guess, friend. But this passage names a different stop. The group went as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). Memphis never comes up in these verses.

Zoan is a fair guess, but the text here says they went as far as Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:7). Zoan never comes up in these verses, friend. Tahpanhes is where this stop on the trip ends, and it's where the LORD's word finds Jeremiah next.

That's it, baker. The LORD tells Jeremiah to pick up some large stones and bury them in the clay of the brick pavement in the sight of the Jews (Jeremiah 43:9). It's a message with no words yet, meant to be seen. I think that gets people asking questions.

That one comes from another Jeremiah scene. The LORD once told him to make straps and yoke bars and put them on his neck (Jeremiah 27:2). Not this time, friend. In Tahpanhes he's told to bury large stones in the clay of the brick pavement (Jeremiah 43:9).
I see where your mind went. But the stones aren't buried at Solomon's palace. The LORD points Jeremiah to the entrance to Pharaoh's palace at Tahpanhes (Jeremiah 43:9). We're in Egypt now, baker.

That's the one, baker. The LORD of Hosts says, “I will send for My servant Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon…” (Jeremiah 43:10). Nebuchadnezzar is the king the remnant was told not to fear (Jeremiah 42:11). The stones are about him.

Cyrus does show up later in the Bible, where the LORD stirs his spirit to make a proclamation (Ezra 1:1). He isn't the one in this message, though. Here the LORD says He will send for Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon (Jeremiah 43:10). Right idea with a king, friend, just a different one.

An altar sounds official, but it isn't in these verses. The LORD says He will set Nebuchadnezzar's throne over the stones He has embedded (Jeremiah 43:10). The king will also spread his royal pavilion over them. No altar in sight, baker.

That's not what the LORD says, friend. He says the opposite. Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike down the land of Egypt (Jeremiah 43:11). The LORD had already warned that the sword they feared would catch up with them there (Jeremiah 42:16). I think that one hurts to hear.

Correct, baker. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will come and strike down the land of Egypt (Jeremiah 43:11). So Egypt isn't safe from the king of Babylon. The verse goes on to name death, captivity and the sword for those destined for them (Jeremiah 43:11).
Guarding is the opposite of what the text says, friend. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will burn the temples and take their gods as captives (Jeremiah 43:12). So the answer is burn.

That's right, baker. The LORD says Nebuchadnezzar will wrap himself with the land of Egypt as a shepherd wraps himself in his garment, and depart from there “unscathed.” (Jeremiah 43:12). That's the LORD's word on how the king leaves. He leaves without a scratch.
